finding.claim: A request with a parameterized urlencoded Content-Type (e.g. 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded; charset=utf-8') skips request body parsing, so ARGS_POST and REQUEST_BODY are never populated and body rules do not fire, while a backend form parser still reads the body. Bypass of body inspection in default configuration when body access is enabled. Not run; verified by reading the code.
finding.source: HTTP request Content-Type header (attacker-controlled), lowercased at transaction.go:385
finding.sink: Body processor selection (reqbodyProcessor) and body rule evaluation on ARGS_POST / REQUEST_BODY at transaction.go:1100-1120

trace.note: Content-Type value is lowercased, no parameter stripping
Exact equality with 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded'; parameterized value fails, reqbodyProcessor is not set to URLENCODED
rbp read from reqbodyProcessor, resulting in empty string
rbp == '' returns early after phase rule evaluation; no body processor runs
Not reached: the URLENCODED processor that would populate ARGS_POST and REQUEST_BODY never runs

finding.guards_checked: Multipart branch (transaction.go:388) uses HasPrefix so it is not affected. No fallback re-derives the type from the raw header. ForceRequestBodyVariable is reset to false at waf.go:210 and only set via ctl, so it does not cover this by default. RequestBodyAccess must be enabled (deployment-dependent). Repo test rules_test.go:752-792 shows charset-bearing Content-Types are expected in real traffic, so the gap is not a deliberate exclusion.

finding.claim: Under RequestBodyLimitAction=ProcessPartial, body bytes past RequestBodyLimit are passed through without inspection. Documented trade-off; exploitable only when an operator selects ProcessPartial. Low severity, configuration-dependent.
finding.sink: Request body rule evaluation (uninspected tail of body)

trace.note: On limit reached with ProcessPartial, writes only up to the limit and runs ProcessRequestBody
On subsequent WriteRequestBody calls at the limit, returns nil without buffering or inspecting further bytes

finding.guards_checked: Default RequestBodyLimitAction is not ProcessPartial, so this requires explicit operator opt-in. Behavior is documented.

finding.claim: The @inspectFile operator fails open: on timeout or any execution error it returns false (no match), so a deny rule is bypassed if an attacker can make the external scanner time out or fail. The doc comment (lines 22-26) also contradicts the code on which output means match: the code returns true for any non-'1' output (line 58). Low-medium, requires a rule using @inspectFile.
finding.source: Request value (e.g. REQUEST_BODY, FILES_TMPNAMES) passed as argv[1] to the external program, attacker-controlled size and content
finding.sink: Verdict of the external scanner used by a deny rule (return value of Evaluate)

trace.note: 10s context timeout set on the external program run
exec.CommandContext(o.path, value): value is an argv element, no shell
On deadline exceeded or err != nil, returns false (no match, fail-open)
Otherwise returns true for any non-'1' first output byte, contradicting the doc comment semantics at lines 22-26

finding.guards_checked: No shell is used, so no shell injection. Program path comes from rule-author configuration, not the request. Residual concern: attacker-controlled value is passed as an argument without a '--' separator, so leading '-' could be interpreted as an option by the scanner.
